0625.name: Physics
0625.description: Cambridge IGCSE Physics (0625) covers the fundamental principles of physics: mechanics, thermal physics, waves, electricity, magnetism, and nuclear and space physics. The Extended tier adds mathematical depth to every topic.
study_guide: Read each subtopic note, then practise the matching past-paper questions under timed conditions.
Tick each syllabus learning outcome on the chapter checklist once you can answer it from memory.
Focus on command words: State = one fact; Describe = several sentences; Explain = give reasons; Calculate = show all working.
Extended tier students must also master the Supplement subtopics (marked with a blue badge).

chapters.name: Physical quantities & measurement
learning_outcomes: Describe the use of rulers and measuring cylinders to find a length or a volume
Describe how to measure a variety of time intervals using clocks and digital timers
Determine an average value for a small distance or time interval by measuring multiples (including the period of a pendulum)
Understand that a scalar quantity has magnitude only and a vector quantity has magnitude and direction
Know the scalar quantities: distance, speed, time, mass, energy and temperature
Know the vector quantities: force, weight, velocity, acceleration, momentum, electric field strength and gravitational field strength
Determine, by calculation or graphically, the resultant of two vectors at right angles (forces or velocities only)

common_scenarios: Pendulum timing experiment — describe how to measure the period accurately
Parallax error — describe how to read a ruler or measuring cylinder correctly
Vector addition — calculate the resultant of two perpendicular forces or velocities
Reading a measuring cylinder — identify and correct the error in a diagram
exam_insight.tip: Measurement 'describe' questions award one mark per correct procedural step. Always state: the instrument used, how you read it (eye level, bottom of meniscus), and how you reduce error.

chapters.name: Motion
learning_outcomes: Define and calculate average speed using speed = distance / time
Sketch and interpret distance-time graphs: gradient = speed
Define velocity as speed in a given direction
Define acceleration as change in velocity divided by time; calculate using a = (v – u) / t
Sketch and interpret speed-time graphs: gradient = acceleration, area under graph = distance
Apply the equations of uniformly accelerated motion to solve problems (Supplement)
State that the acceleration of free fall near the Earth's surface is approximately 10 m/s²
Describe terminal velocity and explain the forces acting on a falling object

common_scenarios: Read a distance-time graph — calculate speed from the gradient of a section
Read a speed-time graph — calculate acceleration and total distance travelled
Apply a SUVAT equation to find unknown velocity, time or distance (Extended)
Describe why a sky-diver reaches terminal velocity and what changes when the parachute opens
exam_insight.tip: In graph questions, always show gradient working clearly: Δy ÷ Δx with units. For area under a speed-time graph, split into rectangles and triangles and show each area calculation separately.

chapters.name: Mass & weight
learning_outcomes: State that mass is a measure of the quantity of matter in an object
State that weight is a gravitational force on an object due to a gravitational field
Calculate weight using W = mg
Know that g ≈ 10 N/kg at the Earth's surface
Distinguish between mass and weight: mass is constant everywhere; weight depends on g
Describe the use of a spring balance to measure weight and a beam balance to measure mass
Know that g varies on different planets and moons

common_scenarios: Calculate the weight of an object on Earth or the Moon using W = mg
Explain why an astronaut's mass is unchanged on the Moon but weight is different
State which instrument measures mass (beam balance) vs weight (spring balance)
Find g from a given weight and mass
exam_insight.tip: Mass never changes — it is always in kg. Weight is a force, always in N, and depends on g. Never write 'mass = 10 N'. On the Moon, g ≈ 1.6 N/kg, so weight is roughly one-sixth of the Earth value.

chapters.name: Density
learning_outcomes: Define density as mass per unit volume: ρ = m/V
Recall and use the equation ρ = m/V to calculate density, mass or volume
State the SI unit of density (kg/m³) and the alternative unit g/cm³; convert between them
Describe how to determine the density of a regular solid using a ruler and balance
Describe how to determine the density of an irregular solid using the displacement method (measuring cylinder or eureka can)
Describe how to determine the density of a liquid using a measuring cylinder and balance
Predict whether an object will float or sink based on its density relative to the liquid

common_scenarios: Calculate density given mass and volume, or find mass/volume given density
Describe the experimental method to find density of an irregular solid by displacement
Predict floating or sinking from density data
Convert between g/cm³ and kg/m³
exam_insight.tip: For the displacement experiment, always state: measure initial and final water levels, subtract to find volume of solid, then use ρ = m/V. Examiners expect you to mention reading the meniscus at eye level and ensuring the solid is fully submerged.

chapters.name: Forces
learning_outcomes: State the effects a force can have on an object: change shape, speed or direction
Distinguish between contact forces (friction, normal reaction, tension) and non-contact forces (gravity, magnetic, electrostatic)
Calculate the resultant of forces acting along the same straight line
Draw and interpret free body diagrams with labelled force arrows
State Newton's First Law: an object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it
Recall and use F = ma to calculate resultant force, mass or acceleration
State Newton's Third Law and identify Newton's Third Law pairs
State that extension is directly proportional to force, within the limit of proportionality (Hooke's Law)
Recall and use F = ke, where k is the spring constant
Describe and interpret a force–extension graph including the limit of proportionality and elastic limit
Define the moment of a force as M = F × d and use the principle of moments for equilibrium
Define centre of gravity and describe how to find it for a flat lamina by suspension
Explain the conditions that affect stability in terms of centre of gravity and base area

common_scenarios: Calculate acceleration using F = ma given driving force and friction; or find the resultant force
Identify a Newton's Third Law pair and explain why the forces do not cancel
Principle of moments calculation: find unknown force or distance for a balanced beam
Describe the experiment to investigate Hooke's Law and find the spring constant from the graph gradient
Explain why an object is more stable after its base is widened or its centre of gravity is lowered
exam_insight.tip: Newton's Third Law pairs are a frequent trap: the pair must be the same type of force, equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and acting on different objects. The weight of a book and the table's normal reaction on the book are NOT a Third Law pair — they are balanced forces on the same object.

chapters.name: Momentum
learning_outcomes: Define momentum as the product of mass and velocity: p = mv
Recall and use the equation p = mv, rearranging to find mass or velocity
State that momentum is a vector quantity with the same direction as velocity
State the principle of conservation of momentum: total momentum is conserved in the absence of external forces
Apply conservation of momentum to collisions and explosions in a straight line
Distinguish between elastic collisions (KE conserved) and inelastic collisions (KE not conserved)
Define impulse as the product of force and time: impulse = FΔt = Δp
Use F = Δp/Δt to calculate force, change in momentum or time of contact
Find the impulse from the area under a force–time graph
Explain how increasing the time of a collision reduces the force, with examples from crash safety

common_scenarios: Two trolleys collide and stick together — find common velocity using conservation of momentum
Gun/rocket recoil — system initially at rest, find recoil velocity
Head-on collision with objects in opposite directions — careful sign convention required
Airbag/crumple zone — explain in terms of impulse (same Δp, larger Δt, smaller F)
F–t graph — find change in momentum from the area under the curve
exam_insight.tip: Extended students must always show momentum before and after in a clear layout. A common error is forgetting that velocity is a vector — objects moving in opposite directions need opposite signs. Impulse questions often carry 3 marks: state the formula, substitute correctly, include correct unit (N·s or kg·m/s).

chapters.name: Energy, work & power
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe different energy stores: gravitational PE, kinetic, chemical, thermal, elastic, nuclear, electromagnetic
State the principle of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed
Describe energy transfer chains for common situations (falling object, burning fuel, pendulum)
Draw and interpret Sankey diagrams with arrow widths proportional to energy amounts
Recall and use W = Fd to calculate work done, force, or distance
State that work done equals energy transferred and understand the conditions for work to be done
Find work done from the area under a force–distance graph
Recall and use P = W/t = E/t to calculate power, energy, or time
Use P = Fv for an object moving at constant velocity under a constant force (Extended)
Recall and use ΔE_p = mgΔh for gravitational potential energy
Recall and use E_k = ½mv² for kinetic energy
Apply conservation of energy to convert between GPE and KE (with and without energy losses)
Calculate efficiency as useful energy output ÷ total energy input; use as a fraction or percentage
Use efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input (Extended)

common_scenarios: A falling object — calculate KE at a given height using ΔE_p = E_k; or find speed using v = √(2gh)
A motor or engine — calculate efficiency given input and output energy or power
Stair-climbing experiment — calculate power from mass, height, and time
Sankey diagram — read off useful and wasted energy; calculate efficiency
P = Fv — find engine power given driving force and constant speed (Extended)
exam_insight.tip: Always check whether air resistance is 'ignored' or 'not negligible' — if ignored, all GPE converts to KE. If air resistance is present, some energy is lost to thermal: KE gained < GPE lost. For efficiency, always divide by the TOTAL input, never the useful output.

chapters.name: Pressure
learning_outcomes: Define pressure as force per unit area: P = F/A
Recall and use P = F/A; convert area units between cm² and m²
Explain everyday examples of high and low pressure in terms of force and contact area
State that pressure in a liquid increases with depth and depends on the density of the liquid
State that pressure at a given depth in a liquid acts equally in all directions
Recall and use P = hρg to calculate pressure, depth, or density in a liquid
Describe how atmospheric pressure arises from the weight of air above, and decreases with altitude
Describe how a mercury barometer works and how the height of mercury indicates atmospheric pressure
Use h = P/(ρg) to relate atmospheric pressure to the height of a mercury column
Describe and use a U-tube manometer to compare or measure gas pressure

common_scenarios: Calculate pressure on a surface given force and area; or find area or force from pressure
Explain in terms of P = F/A why a design feature increases or decreases pressure (e.g. wide tyres, sharp knife)
Calculate liquid pressure at a given depth using P = hρg; find the depth or density instead
Barometer — describe how it works and explain what happens when taken to a higher altitude
Manometer — find gas pressure given the height difference of liquid levels
exam_insight.tip: P = F/A needs force in newtons (not kg) and area in m² (not cm²). For liquid pressure, the shape of the container is irrelevant — only the vertical depth matters. For barometer questions: higher altitude → less air above → lower atmospheric pressure → shorter mercury column.

2058.name: Islamiat
2058.description: Cambridge O Level Islamiat (2058) covers the Holy Quran, Hadith and Sunnah, Islamic beliefs, worship (Ibadat), and the history of early Islam — from the life of the Prophet ﷺ through the first four caliphs.
study_guide: Learn Quranic verses with their surah name and approximate verse number — examiners award marks for citing references correctly.
For Hadith, always state the narrator or collection (e.g. Bukhari, Muslim, Tirmidhi) when you quote it in an answer.
For essay questions, structure every point: Reference → Explanation → Relevance to the question.
Paper 2 history questions ask you to 'evaluate' or 'assess the importance of' — give multiple reasons, then a supported conclusion.

extended.name: Written Paper
extended.questions: 5 questions (answer all); Quran, Hadith, Belief, Worship

core.name: Written Paper
core.questions: 5 questions (answer 3); Seerah, early caliphs, spread of Islam

chapters.name: Quranic References & Hadith
learning_outcomes: Recall and quote key Quranic verses relevant to each syllabus topic
State the surah name and approximate verse number for quoted ayat
Recall and quote key Hadith with their narrator or collection
Explain the relevance and lesson of each reference to the question asked
Use references correctly to support arguments in extended essay answers

common_scenarios: Quote a Quranic verse that shows the importance of prayer — give surah and meaning
Use Hadith to support a point about the Prophet's character or conduct
Explain what a verse reveals about the nature of Allah
Quote evidence for the importance of fasting, zakat or hajj
exam_insight.tip: Each reference earns you marks only if you also explain what it means and link it to the question. A bare quotation with no explanation typically scores 1 mark at most.

chapters.name: Battles of Islam
chapters.section: Paper 2 — Life of the Prophet ﷺ
learning_outcomes: State the date, location and key participants of each battle
Describe the background causes and events of each battle
Explain the outcome and immediate aftermath of each battle
Assess the significance of each battle for the growth and survival of Islam
Identify the lessons that Muslims can draw from each battle

common_scenarios: Describe the events of the Battle of Badr — causes, events, outcome
Why did the Muslims face difficulties at Uhud? What lessons did it teach?
How important was the strategy of digging a trench at Khandaq?
Evaluate the significance of the Conquest of Makkah for the spread of Islam
exam_insight.tip: For 'assess the importance' questions, always give at least three distinct reasons and a judgement sentence at the end: 'Overall, the most important factor was… because…'

4024.name: Mathematics D
4024.description: Cambridge O Level Mathematics D (4024) develops algebraic, geometric and statistical reasoning across two papers. Paper 1 is non-calculator; Paper 2 allows a scientific calculator and demands structured written working.
study_guide: Sketch graphs freehand first — a correctly shaped curve with key points labelled earns method marks even if the plot is imperfect.
Show every step of working in Paper 2; method marks are available independently of the final answer.
After solving an equation algebraically, substitute your answer back in to verify it is correct.
Memorise key graph shapes, their equations and features (intercepts, asymptotes, turning points) — they appear across every series.

chapters.name: Graphs of Functions
learning_outcomes: Recognise and sketch y = ax^n for n = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 and simple sums of these
Identify and state the coordinates of turning points, intercepts and asymptotes
Sketch and interpret graphs of the form y = ab^x (exponential growth and decay)
Use a graph to solve an equation by reading off intersection points
Sketch the graph of a function after a given transformation (translation, stretch)

common_scenarios: Sketch y = x³ − 3x showing intercepts and turning points
Use the graph of y = 2^x to solve 2^x = 5
Sketch the graph of y = k/x and identify its asymptotes
Describe the transformation that maps y = f(x) onto y = f(x+2)
exam_insight.tip: For 'sketch' questions you do not need perfect accuracy — but you must show the correct shape, cross the right axes, and mark key coordinates. Missing labels lose marks.
